implementation_notes: Since C++17 std::optional<T> is the standard realization: it stores the contained value inside the wrapper (no heap allocation, models an object rather than a pointer), and the library documents its purpose as the return value of a function that may fail, explicitly as more readable than std::pair<T, bool>. value() throws std::bad_optional_access on an empty optional, value_or() supplies the default, and C++23 adds the monadic operations and_then/transform/or_else. The classic hand-written Maybe is replaced by the standard type; it is still justified only where the standard is older than C++17 (then boost::optional) or where the representation must be packed.
pitfalls: An optional holding a reference-like value (string_view, span, pointer into a container) does not extend any lifetime; the dangling access survives the wrapper.
operator* on a disengaged optional is undefined behaviour and value() throws std::bad_optional_access; value_or, if (opt) and the monadic operations are the checked paths.
optional<T> costs the tag plus padding: in large arrays or hot loops a spare-bit representation can be measurably smaller (that optimization is not guaranteed here).
Returning optional<T> for an expensive T constructs the object even for the empty case unless the empty value is produced with nullopt and the filled one with emplace.

variants.name: std::optional with C++23 monadic operations
variants.implementation_notes: C++23 adds and_then, transform and or_else, which turn a chain of 'if present, continue' checks into a single expression and let the whole pipeline collapse to nullopt at the first empty stage. Choose it where the toolchain is C++23 and lookup/parse pipelines are common; the roles do not change, only the spelling of the propagation. C++20's std::ranges and the error type std::expected are the natural neighbours, and std::expected should be preferred as soon as the caller needs a reason.
variants.code_sketch:
auto note = lookup_user(id)                 // std::optional<User>
    .and_then([](const User& u) { return u.address(); })
    .transform([](const Address& a) { return a.city(); })
    .value_or("unknown");
pitfalls: The monadic operations are C++23-only: mixing them into a C++17 code base breaks the build, so the floor belongs in the project's standard setting.
or_else must return an optional of the same type; using it to report why the value was missing loses the reason just like value_or does.

variants.name: Boost.Optional before C++17
variants.implementation_notes: Before C++17, boost::optional<T> is the de-facto standard realization and the direct ancestor of std::optional: the same safe-bool conversion, operator*/operator->, value_or and get_value_or, plus support for optional references that std::optional does not have. The library documents the canonical case - a configuration parameter that may be absent while every value of the type is legitimate. Choose it where the standard library is older than C++17 or where optional references are needed; migration to std::optional is mechanical otherwise.
pitfalls: boost::optional and std::optional have slightly different interfaces (get_value_or, optional references); mixing both in one code base confuses overload resolution and review.
Boost is a heavyweight dependency for a type that the standard library now provides - keep it only while the standard floor prevents the migration.
